vignette:
The Weight of the Kitchen

Maria is forty-three years old and has spent the better part of two decades building a career around the controlled chaos of a professional kitchen. She is the kind of woman who thrives under pressure — who can manage six burners, a full dining room, and a team of line cooks without losing her composure. Two years ago, that sense of mastery collapsed entirely when she was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia.

The diagnosis came quickly and without warning. Maria had gone to her GP with what she assumed was persistent fatigue from overwork — long shifts, poor sleep, the physical toll of standing for ten hours a day. Within a week of her bloodwork, she was admitted to hospital and told she would need immediate chemotherapy. She remembers sitting on the edge of a hospital bed in a paper gown, watching a haematologist's mouth move, and feeling as though the sound in the room had been turned off. Her partner, David, was holding her hand, but she could not feel it.

The months that followed were brutal. Maria underwent two rounds of intensive chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant. There were nights when she genuinely believed she would not survive — nights when her fever spiked and nurses moved around her with a quiet urgency that told her more than any doctor's words. She lay in isolation for weeks, separated from David by glass and gloves, eating nothing, unable to read or watch television, existing in a suspended state between living and dying. She describes those weeks as "being buried alive while still breathing."

She is now in remission. Her oncologist uses words like encouraging and stable, and by every measurable standard, Maria has recovered. She returned to her restaurant eight months ago, which everyone around her framed as a triumph. It does not feel like one.

Standing at the pass, she finds herself scanning the kitchen for threats she cannot name. The smell of antiseptic cleaning fluid — standard in any commercial kitchen — sends a cold wave through her chest that she has learned to mask by turning away and gripping the edge of the counter. When one of her sous-chefs moves too quickly past her, or when a pot boils over and steam rises unexpectedly, her heart lurches into a rhythm that feels nothing like excitement. She has burned herself twice in the past month, not from carelessness but from the strange dissociation that overtakes her without warning — moments when she is suddenly not in her kitchen at all, but back in that hospital room, watching the IV drip.

At home, Maria sleeps poorly and briefly. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, certain something is wrong with her body. She catalogues sensations — a twinge in her hip, a headache, a patch of dry skin — and lies awake constructing worst-case scenarios until her alarm goes off. David has learned not to reach for her in these moments, having discovered early on that being touched while she is in that state makes things worse. She appreciates his patience and simultaneously feels a profound guilt about the distance that has grown between them.

She rarely speaks about the illness directly. With her staff, she is the same demanding, exacting chef she has always been — perhaps more so, as though sheer professional intensity can hold the other thing at bay. With David, she deflects with dark humour. With herself, in the quiet of the early morning kitchen before service begins, she sometimes stands very still and wonders whether the person who walked into that hospital two years ago ever actually walked back out, or whether the woman plating dishes and calling orders is simply a very convincing reconstruction.

Maria does not think of herself as someone who is struggling. She thinks of herself as someone who survived, and she has not yet understood that these two things are not the same.
